hints: Think about why NMR needs a zero point for chemical shift and a solvent with no $^{1}\text{H}$ signal to avoid extra peaks.
walkthrough:
Set the zero for chemical shift**
You and I always measure chemical shift $\delta$ relative to something. That something is tetramethylsilane, $(\text{CH}_3)_4\text{Si}$, called TMS. It gives one sharp singlet from 12 equivalent protons, well away from most signals, and is set as $\delta = 0$ ppm.

Choose a proton-free solvent**
If you dissolved A in ordinary $\text{CHCl}_3$ or $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, the solvent protons would give a huge peak. So we use a deuterated solvent such as $\text{CDCl}_3$ or $\text{D}_2\text{O}$. Deuterium ($^{2}\text{H}$) does not show in the $^{1}\text{H}$ NMR spectrum, leaving only the peaks of A visible.

Final answer: reference: tetramethylsilane, TMS, $(\text{CH}_3)_4\text{Si}$
solvent: $\text{CDCl}_3$ or $\text{D}_2\text{O}$

hints: Label each carbon in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCO}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ and look for any pair made identical by symmetry, especially in the isopropyl group.
walkthrough:
Draw out compound A clearly**
Let me redraw A with you: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{C}(=\text{O})\text{OCH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$. Count the carbons: 2 in the ethyl part, 2 carbonyl carbons, 1 CH and 2 $\text{CH}_3$ in the isopropyl ester part. That is 7 carbon atoms in total.

Spot the equivalent pair**
Now ask, are all 7 in different environments? The two $\text{CH}_3$ groups on the $\text{OCH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$ are attached to the same CH and are free to rotate, so they are chemically equivalent. Every other carbon is unique: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_2$, keto $\text{C}=\text{O}$, ester $\text{C}=\text{O}$, and OCH. So $7 - 1 = 6$ distinct environments, giving 6 peaks in $^{13}\text{C}$ NMR.

hints: Start by dividing A into its four proton groups: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$, $\text{CH}_2$, $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}$, and $\text{OCH}$, and match deshielding to $\delta$ with OCH most downfield.
Recall the n+1 rule, splitting pattern is determined by the number of protons on the adjacent carbon atoms.
Use the given integration of 6H at $\delta$ 1.50 to identify the two equivalent $\text{CH}_3$ groups of the isopropyl unit and work out what splits them.
Check total proton count adds to 12H and that the $\text{OCH}$ proton sees 6 neighbouring protons, giving a septet often labelled as multiplet.
walkthrough:
Find the four proton environments**
Talk this through with me. A is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCO}_2\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$. The protons fall into four sets: ethyl $\text{CH}_3$ (3H), ethyl $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C}=\text{O}$ (2H), isopropyl $2 \times \text{CH}_3$ (6H equivalent), and isopropyl OCH (1H). That matches the statement of four different chemical environments. Total $3+2+6+1 = 12$H.

Assign chemical shifts by deshielding**
Protons near electronegative oxygen or carbonyl are pulled downfield to higher $\delta$. The most deshielded is the $\text{OCH}$ proton directly on carbon attached to O, so $\delta$ 3.75 is OCH (1H). Next is $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C}=\text{O}$, so $\delta$ 2.85 is $\text{CH}_2$ (2H). The two alkyl $\text{CH}_3$ types appear upfield: $\delta$ 1.50 integrating to 6H must be the two equivalent isopropyl $\text{CH}_3$ groups, leaving $\delta$ 1.10 (3H) as the ethyl $\text{CH}_3$.

Apply the n+1 rule for splitting**
Splitting depends only on protons on adjacent carbons. Ethyl $\text{CH}_3$ at 1.10 sees $\text{CH}_2$ with 2H, so $n+1 = 3$, triplet. Ethyl $\text{CH}_2$ at 2.85 sees $\text{CH}_3$ with 3H, so $n+1 = 4$, quartet. Isopropyl $\text{CH}_3$ groups at 1.50 see the single CH (1H), so $n+1 = 2$, doublet. The OCH at 3.75 sees six equivalent protons from the two $\text{CH}_3$ groups, so $n+1 = 7$, a septet which is recorded as multiplet.

Complete the table and cross check**
Put it together: 1.10 triplet, 2 adjacent, 3H. 1.50 doublet, 1 adjacent, 6H given. 2.85 quartet, 3 adjacent, 2H. 3.75 multiplet, 6 adjacent, 1H. Notice the symmetry: the 3H triplet pairs with the 2H quartet as a classic ethyl pattern, and the 6H doublet pairs with the 1H multiplet as a classic isopropyl pattern. That is a great way to confirm you are correct.

Final answer: $\delta$ 1.10: triplet, 2 protons on adjacent carbons, 3 $^{1}\text{H}$ atoms; $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$
$\delta$ 1.50: doublet, 1 proton on adjacent carbon, 6 $^{1}\text{H}$ atoms; $\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)_2$
$\delta$ 2.85: quartet, 3 protons on adjacent carbons, 2 $^{1}\text{H}$ atoms; $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2$
$\delta$ 3.75: multiplet (septet), 6 protons on adjacent carbons, 1 $^{1}\text{H}$ atom; $\text{OCH}$
